title: The verb be: am, is, and are
content: The verb be describes identity, feelings, jobs, and states. Use am with I, is with he/she/it or one person, and are with you/we/they or plural nouns. Make a negative with not: I am not tired; She is not at home; They are not ready. In questions, put be before the subject: Are you a student? Is he happy? Short answers use the subject and be: Yes, I am. No, they aren't. Do not add do or does to a be question. Common mistake: She are a teacher. Correct: She is a teacher.

title: Present simple for routines
content: Use the present simple for habits, routines, and facts. With I/you/we/they, use the base verb: I study English. With he/she/it, usually add -s or -es: She studies at night; He watches TV. For negatives, use do not (don't) or does not (doesn't) plus the base verb: We don't work on Sunday; He doesn't drive. For questions, use Do/Does + subject + base verb: Do you like tea? Does Mai live here? After does, do not add -s to the main verb. Common mistake: He doesn't likes coffee. Correct: He doesn't like coffee.

title: A, an, and the
content: Use a or an with one singular countable noun when it is not specific or is mentioned for the first time: a book, an apple. Choose a or an by sound: an hour, a university. Use the when the listener knows which person or thing you mean, or when it is unique in the context: I saw a dog. The dog was brown. We also use the with some shared references, such as the sun. Do not normally use a/an with plural or uncountable nouns: books, water. Common mistake: I have a homework. Correct: I have homework.

title: Regular plural nouns
content: Most countable nouns form the plural with -s: book/books, student/students. Add -es after many endings in s, sh, ch, or x: bus/buses, watch/watches, box/boxes. For many nouns ending in z, double the z and add -es: quiz/quizzes. For a consonant + y, change y to -ies: city/cities. For a vowel + y, add -s: day/days. Some nouns are irregular and must be learned: child/children, person/people, man/men. Use a plural verb with plural nouns: The keys are here. Common mistake: two childs. Correct: two children. Some nouns have the same singular and plural form, such as sheep.

title: There is and there are
content: Use there is with a singular countable noun or an uncountable noun: There is a chair in the room. There is some milk in the fridge. Use there are with plural nouns: There are two chairs. Make a negative with not: There isn't a bus stop nearby; There aren't any clean cups. For questions, put is or are first: Is there a bank near here? Are there any messages? Use some in many positive statements and any in many questions and negatives. Common mistake: There is three books. Correct: There are three books.

title: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
content: Use the past simple for a finished action at a finished time: We visited Hue last summer. Regular verbs usually add -ed: clean/cleaned; verbs ending in consonant + y change y to -ied: study/studied. Many common verbs are irregular: go/went, see/saw, have/had. Use did not (didn't) + base verb for negatives: She didn't call. Use Did + subject + base verb for questions: Did they arrive? The main verb stays in its base form after did. Common mistake: Did you went home? Correct: Did you go home?

title: Present continuous for actions happening now
content: Use the present continuous for an action happening now or around now. Form it with am/is/are + verb-ing: I am reading; Lan is working; They are waiting. Add not after be for a negative: He isn't sleeping. Put be before the subject for a question: Are you listening? Spelling often doubles a final consonant after a short stressed vowel: run/running; drop final e: make/making. Many state verbs, such as know and believe, are not usually used in the continuous for their ordinary meanings: I know the answer. Common mistake: She is work now. Correct: She is working now.

title: Countable and uncountable nouns
content: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms: one bottle, two bottles. Uncountable nouns are not normally counted as individual items: water, rice, information. Use many with plural countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, especially in questions and negatives: How many eggs? How much rice? A lot of can be used with both: a lot of books, a lot of time. Use a piece of or a bottle of to count an amount of an uncountable noun. Common mistake: many information. Correct: much information or a lot of information. Some nouns can be countable or uncountable with a change in meaning, such as coffee (a drink or a serving).

title: Comparative adjectives
content: Use a comparative adjective to compare two people or things. Short adjectives usually take -er: small/smaller, fast/faster. For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to -ier: easy/easier. Longer adjectives usually use more: more comfortable. Irregular forms include good/better and bad/worse. Use than before the second item: This road is wider than that road. Use as + adjective + as to say two things are equal: My bag is as heavy as yours. Common mistake: more easier. Correct: easier. Do not use more and -er together for the same adjective.

title: Be going to for plans and predictions
content: Use be going to + base verb for a plan or intention decided before speaking: We are going to visit our aunt. Use it for a prediction based on evidence you can see now: Look at those clouds. It is going to rain. Change be to match the subject: I am going to study; She is going to study; They are going to study. Make a negative with not after be and a question by moving be before the subject: Is he going to join us? Common mistake: She is going to studies. Correct: She is going to study. For a future event with no prior plan, will may be more natural.

title: Present perfect for life experience
content: Use the present perfect to talk about experience up to now when the exact finished time is not stated. Form it with have/has + past participle: I have visited Da Nang; She has tried sushi. Many past participles are irregular, such as been, eaten, and written. Use ever in many questions about experience and never for an experience that has not happened: Have you ever flown? I have never flown. Do not use a finished-time expression such as yesterday with this experience use; use the past simple instead: I visited Da Nang last year. Common mistake: She have seen it. Correct: She has seen it.

title: Present perfect and past simple
content: Use the past simple when you say or ask about a finished time in the past: I saw that film last week. Use the present perfect when the time is not specified or the period continues to now: I have seen that film; She has worked here for two years. Compare: Did you eat breakfast at 7? (finished time) and Have you eaten breakfast yet? (relevant now). For an action that started in the past and continues, use for with a duration and since with a starting point: for two years, since 2024. Common mistake: I have met him yesterday. Correct: I met him yesterday.

title: Must, have to, and should
content: Use must or have to for a strong obligation. Have to changes with the subject and tense: She has to leave; We had to wait. Must is followed by the base verb: You must wear a helmet. Use should for advice or a recommendation: You should get some rest. The meanings of mustn't and don't have to are different: mustn't means something is prohibited; don't have to means it is not necessary. Common mistake: He must to go. Correct: He must go. In everyday use, have to is common for obligations, while must often expresses a strong rule or the speaker's view.

title: First conditional
content: Use the first conditional for a real or possible future situation and its result. The if-clause normally uses the present simple; the main clause often uses will + base verb: If it rains, we will stay inside. The if-clause can come first or second. When it comes first, use a comma between the clauses. Do not normally put will in the if-clause: If I will have time is usually incorrect for this pattern. Use If I have time, I will call you. Other modal verbs or imperatives can appear in the result: If you finish early, you can leave. Common mistake: If she will come, I will tell her. Correct: If she comes, I will tell her.

title: Defining relative clauses
content: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing we mean. Use who for people and which for things; that can often replace who or which in a defining clause: The person who called is my cousin. The book that I borrowed is useful. Do not put commas around a defining relative clause because the information is needed to identify the noun. When the relative pronoun is the object, it can often be omitted: The song (that) we heard was beautiful. Do not omit it when it is the subject: The woman who lives next door is a doctor. Common mistake: The student, who sits near me, is in my class when the clause is meant to identify which student.
